Atomic Orbitals

What you need to know

  • An atomic orbital is one stationary state of a one-electron atom, ψnlm=Rnl(r) Ylm(θ,ϕ)\psi_{nlm} = R_{nl}(r)\,Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)ψnlm​=Rnl​(r)Ylm​(θ,ϕ), named by nnn and the letter of lll: 1s, 2p, 3d. Lecture 5.1 solved for them. This lecture draws them, and learns to read the drawings.

  • “Where is the electron?” has three answers. ∣ψ∣2 dV\lvert\psi\rvert^2\,dV∣ψ∣2dV is the probability of finding it in a small volume; the radial distribution P(r)=r2Rnl2P(r) = r^2R_{nl}^2P(r)=r2Rnl2​ is the probability per unit length of finding it at distance rrr, at any angle (the r2r^2r2 is the area of the shell); ∣Ylm∣2\lvert Y_l^m\rvert^2∣Ylm​∣2 is the probability per unit solid angle of finding it in a direction. The 1s density is largest at the nucleus, but P(r)P(r)P(r) peaks at a0a_0a0​: the most probable distance. The average distance is 32a0\tfrac{3}{2}a_023​a0​, and 90% of the electron lies inside 2.66 a02.66\,a_02.66a0​.

  • Sizes grow as n2a0/Zn^2a_0/Zn2a0​/Z. For l=n−1l = n - 1l=n−1 the most probable distance is exactly Bohr’s n2a0/Zn^2a_0/Zn2a0​/Z; s states keep small inner lobes close to the nucleus, which is why 2s lies below 2p once there are other electrons (Chapter 7).

  • The YlmY_l^mYlm​ with m≠0m \neq 0m=0 are complex and their densities are rings around zzz. Because the 2l+12l + 12l+1 states of one nnn and lll have the same energy, any combination of them is again a stationary state, and the combinations (Yl−m∓Ylm)/2(Y_l^{-m} \mp Y_l^{m})/\sqrt{2}(Yl−m​∓Ylm​)/2​ are real orbitals that point along axes: pxp_xpx​, pyp_ypy​, pzp_zpz​ and the five ddd. They keep EEE and L2L^2L2 but have no definite LzL_zLz​.

  • Nodes: n−l−1n - l - 1n−l−1 radial nodes (spheres) plus lll angular nodes (planes or cones), n−1n - 1n−1 in all. A boundary surface encloses 90% of the probability; it is what the textbook drawings show.

An orbital is a one-electron wavefunction¶

Lecture 5.1 ended with every state of the hydrogenlike atom, ψnlm=Rnl(r) Ylm(θ,ϕ)\psi_{nlm} = R_{nl}(r)\,Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)ψnlm​=Rnl​(r)Ylm​(θ,ϕ), labelled by n=1,2,…n = 1, 2, \dotsn=1,2,…, l=0,…,n−1l = 0, \dots, n - 1l=0,…,n−1 and m=−l,…,lm = -l, \dots, lm=−l,…,l. Chemists call each of these functions an atomic orbital and name it by nnn and the letter of lll:

nnnlllorbitalshow manyenergy
101s1−Eh/2-E_h/2−Eh​/2
20, 12s, 2p1+3=41 + 3 = 41+3=4−Eh/8-E_h/8−Eh​/8
30, 1, 23s, 3p, 3d1+3+5=91 + 3 + 5 = 91+3+5=9−Eh/18-E_h/18−Eh​/18

The word deserves care. An orbital is a wavefunction of one electron, not a path: nothing orbits. For hydrogen the orbitals are exact; for every other atom the word is kept for the one-electron functions out of which the many-electron state is built, an approximation that Chapter 7 makes precise. Everything a chemist draws about atoms, from the periodic table to a π\piπ bond, is drawn in the language of these functions, so this lecture is about drawing them well: where the electron is, what shape the orbital has, where it vanishes, and what a picture of it does and does not show.

Where is the electron?¶

Three distributions¶

∣ψnlm∣2\lvert\psi_{nlm}\rvert^2∣ψnlm​∣2 is a probability per unit volume (Lecture 3.1). In spherical coordinates (Lecture 4.4) the volume element is dV=r2 dr sin⁡θ dθ dϕdV = r^2\,dr\,\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phidV=r2drsinθdθdϕ, and since ψ\psiψ factors into a radial and an angular part, so does the probability:

Where the electron is: three distributions
∣ψnlm∣2 dV=Rnl2(r) r2 dr⏟distance  ×  ∣Ylm(θ,ϕ)∣2 sin⁡θ dθ dϕ⏟direction\lvert\psi_{nlm}\rvert^2\,dV = \underbrace{R_{nl}^2(r)\,r^2\,dr}_{\text{distance}}\;\times\;\underbrace{\lvert Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)\rvert^2\,\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi}_{\text{direction}}∣ψnlm​∣2dV=distanceRnl2​(r)r2dr​​×direction∣Ylm​(θ,ϕ)∣2sinθdθdϕ​​
(1)
P(r)=r2Rnl2(r),∫0∞P(r) dr=1∣Ylm∣2,∫∣Ylm∣2 sin⁡θ dθ dϕ=1P(r) = r^2R_{nl}^2(r), \qquad \int_0^\infty P(r)\,dr = 1 \qquad\qquad \lvert Y_l^m\rvert^2, \qquad \int\lvert Y_l^m\rvert^2\,\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi = 1P(r)=r2Rnl2​(r),∫0∞​P(r)dr=1∣Ylm​∣2,∫∣Ylm​∣2sinθdθdϕ=1
(2)

  • P(r) drP(r)\,drP(r)dr is the probability of finding the electron between rrr and r+drr + drr+dr, in any direction: the radial distribution

  • ∣Ylm∣2 dΩ\lvert Y_l^m\rvert^2\,d\Omega∣Ylm​∣2dΩ is the probability of finding it within the solid angle dΩd\OmegadΩ, at any distance: the angular distribution

Why r2r^2r2: the area of a shell¶

The radial distribution is not the density. Take the ground state, ψ1s=e−r/a0/πa03\psi_{1s} = e^{-r/a_0}/\sqrt{\pi a_0^3}ψ1s​=e−r/a0​/πa03​​. Its density ∣ψ1s∣2\lvert\psi_{1s}\rvert^2∣ψ1s​∣2 is largest at the nucleus and falls off from there. But “at distance rrr” means anywhere on a shell of radius rrr and thickness drdrdr, whose volume is 4πr2 dr4\pi r^2\,dr4πr2dr, and that area starts at zero:

Example: the most probable distance of the 1s electron

Where is P(r)P(r)P(r) largest for the ground state?

With rrr in units of a0a_0a0​, P(r)=4r2e−2rP(r) = 4r^2e^{-2r}P(r)=4r2e−2r, and

dPdr=8r e−2r−8r2e−2r=8r (1−r) e−2r=0⟹r=a0\frac{dP}{dr} = 8r\,e^{-2r} - 8r^2e^{-2r} = 8r\,(1 - r)\,e^{-2r} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = a_0drdP​=8re−2r−8r2e−2r=8r(1−r)e−2r=0⟹r=a0​
(3)

The most probable distance of the electron from the proton is the Bohr radius. Bohr’s orbit of Lecture 1.5 is gone (the state has l=0l = 0l=0, no angular momentum, and the electron is found at every rrr), but its radius survives as the peak of P(r)P(r)P(r): the answer to Problem 8 of the last lecture.

Example: inside the Bohr radius, and the average distance

What fraction of the time is the 1s electron found closer to the nucleus than a0a_0a0​? And what is its average distance?

The antiderivative of 4r2e−2r4r^2e^{-2r}4r2e−2r is −e−2r(2r2+2r+1)-e^{-2r}(2r^2 + 2r + 1)−e−2r(2r2+2r+1) (differentiate to check), so the probability inside a radius xxx (in a0a_0a0​) is

P(r<x)=1−e−2x (2x2+2x+1),P(r<a0)=1−5e−2=0.323P(r < x) = 1 - e^{-2x}\,(2x^2 + 2x + 1), \qquad P(r < a_0) = 1 - 5e^{-2} = 0.323P(r<x)=1−e−2x(2x2+2x+1),P(r<a0​)=1−5e−2=0.323
(4)

Only a third of the time. Two thirds of the time the electron is outside the Bohr radius, because P(r)P(r)P(r) has a long tail. For the average use ∫0∞rke−ar dr=k!/ak+1\int_0^\infty r^ke^{-ar}\,dr = k!/a^{k+1}∫0∞​rke−ardr=k!/ak+1:

⟨r⟩=∫0∞r P(r) dr=4∫0∞r3e−2r dr=4⋅3!24=32 a0\langle r\rangle = \int_0^\infty r\,P(r)\,dr = 4\int_0^\infty r^3e^{-2r}\,dr = 4\cdot\frac{3!}{2^4} = \frac{3}{2}\,a_0⟨r⟩=∫0∞​rP(r)dr=4∫0∞​r3e−2rdr=4⋅243!​=23​a0​
(5)

The average lies beyond the peak, as it does for every lopsided distribution. Three different lengths describe one state: the most probable distance a0a_0a0​, the average 1.5 a01.5\,a_01.5a0​, and the radius inside which 90% of the probability lies, 2.66 a02.66\,a_02.66a0​ (solve P(r<x)=0.9P(r < x) = 0.9P(r<x)=0.9 numerically).

    ax.set_xlabel(r"$r$ ($a_0$)", fontsize=11.5)

axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$P(r) = r^2R_{nl}^2$  (per $a_0$)", fontsize=11.5)

  • One hump for l=n−1l = n - 1l=n−1, at Bohr’s radius. For 1s, 2p and 3d the polynomial is a single power, P∝r2ne−2Zr/na0P \propto r^{2n}e^{-2Zr/na_0}P∝r2ne−2Zr/na0​, and dP/dr=0dP/dr = 0dP/dr=0 gives r=n2a0/Zr = n^2a_0/Zr=n2a0​/Z: the radii of Bohr’s orbits, a0a_0a0​, 4a04a_04a0​, 9a09a_09a0​, reappear as most probable distances (Problem 1).

  • More humps for smaller lll. RnlR_{nl}Rnl​ has n−l−1n - l - 1n−l−1 nodes, so P(r)P(r)P(r) has n−ln - ln−l humps, and the outermost always carries most of the probability. The inner humps of 2s and 3s sit close to the nucleus: an s electron penetrates to small rrr where a p or d electron of the same nnn does not. In hydrogen that changes nothing, since all states of one nnn share one energy. In every other atom the inner electrons screen the nucleus, penetration lets 2s feel more of the nuclear charge than 2p, and 2s drops below 2p: the origin of the aufbau order of Chapter 7.

  • The average distance is the formula of the radial averages dropdown of Lecture 5.1, ⟨r⟩nl=n2a0Z[1+12(1−l(l+1)n2)]\langle r\rangle_{nl} = \dfrac{n^2a_0}{Z}\left[1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{l(l+1)}{n^2}\right)\right]⟨r⟩nl​=Zn2a0​​[1+21​(1−n2l(l+1)​)]: 1.5 a01.5\,a_01.5a0​ for 1s, 6 a06\,a_06a0​ for 2s, 5 a05\,a_05a0​ for 2p. For a given nnn the s state reaches out farthest on average, even though its outer hump peaks beyond the p hump by only a little.

  • Everything scales. P(r)P(r)P(r) for a nucleus ZeZeZe is the hydrogen curve squeezed by 1/Z1/Z1/Z: every length in the table below divides by ZZZ.

Three lengths for the six states, computed by numpy from the radial functions of the last lecture (all in a0a_0a0​, Z=1Z = 1Z=1):

import numpy as np

r = np.linspace(0, 60, 60001); dr = r[1] - r[0]           # r in a0
R = {"1s": 2 * np.exp(-r),
     "2s": (2 - r) * np.exp(-r / 2) / (2 * np.sqrt(2)),
     "2p": r * np.exp(-r / 2) / (2 * np.sqrt(6)),
     "3s": 2 * (27 - 18 * r + 2 * r**2) * np.exp(-r / 3) / (81 * np.sqrt(3)),
     "3p": 4 * (6 - r) * r * np.exp(-r / 3) / (81 * np.sqrt(6)),
     "3d": 4 * r**2 * np.exp(-r / 3) / (81 * np.sqrt(30))}
for name, Rn in R.items():
    P = r**2 * Rn**2                                        # radial distribution, per a0
    inside = np.cumsum(P) * dr                              # probability inside r
    print(f"{name}: r_mp = {r[P.argmax()]:5.2f}   <r> = {np.sum(r * P) * dr:5.2f}   r_90 = {r[np.searchsorted(inside, 0.9)]:5.2f}")

Pick a state, then drag the slider: the darker area is the probability of finding the electron inside the chosen radius. Find the radius that holds half of the 1s electron, and watch how far out 90% of a 3s electron reaches.

The boundary surface¶

An orbital has no edge: P(r)P(r)P(r) falls off exponentially and never reaches zero. To draw a size, chemists draw the surface inside which the electron is found 90% of the time, the boundary surface. For an s orbital it is a sphere; its radius is the last column of the table.

Source

Fig. Left: the 1s radial distribution, with 32% of the probability inside a0a_0a0​ and 90% inside 2.66 a02.66\,a_02.66a0​. Right: the probability inside rrr for every state with n≤3n \leq 3n≤3; the dots mark the 90% radii.

  • The 90% radius of hydrogen’s 1s is 2.66 a0=1412.66\,a_0 = 1412.66a0​=141 pm. Compare the bond length of H2_22​, 74 pm, and the van der Waals radius of a hydrogen atom in a molecule, 120 pm: the orbital pictures in a textbook are drawn to about this size.

  • The 90% radius grows roughly as n2n^2n2 (2.7, 8 to 9, 16 to 19 a0a_0a0​ for n=1n = 1n=1, 2, 3) and shrinks as 1/Z1/Z1/Z: the 1s boundary of He+^++ is at 1.33 a01.33\,a_01.33a0​.

  • For a p or d orbital the boundary surface is not a sphere: it is a surface of constant ∣ψ∣\lvert\psi\rvert∣ψ∣ enclosing 90% of the probability, with the lobes of the angular part. That is the standard orbital drawing, and the 3D widget below draws it.

The shape: the angular part¶

The LzL_zLz​ eigenstates are rings¶

The angular factor of ψnlm\psi_{nlm}ψnlm​ is the spherical harmonic YlmY_l^mYlm​ of Lecture 4.4, and its density ∣Ylm∣2\lvert Y_l^m\rvert^2∣Ylm​∣2 does not depend on ϕ\phiϕ, because Ylm∝eimϕY_l^m \propto e^{im\phi}Ylm​∝eimϕ and ∣eimϕ∣=1\lvert e^{im\phi}\rvert = 1∣eimϕ∣=1. So every state with a definite LzL_zLz​ is symmetric about the zzz axis. For l=1l = 1l=1:

∣Y10∣2=34πcos⁡2θ(a dumbbell along z),∣Y1±1∣2=38πsin⁡2θ(a ring around z)\lvert Y_1^{0}\rvert^2 = \frac{3}{4\pi}\cos^2\theta \quad\text{(a dumbbell along } z\text{)}, \qquad \lvert Y_1^{\pm1}\rvert^2 = \frac{3}{8\pi}\sin^2\theta \quad\text{(a ring around } z\text{)}∣Y10​∣2=4π3​cos2θ(a dumbbell along z),∣Y1±1​∣2=8π3​sin2θ(a ring around z)
(6)

The m=+1m = +1m=+1 and m=−1m = -1m=−1 states have the same density, a ring in the xyxyxy plane; they differ only in the sense in which their phase runs around zzz. These are the states a magnetic field along zzz singles out (Spin). But chemists rarely draw them. A molecule has no zzz axis built in; it has bonds along definite directions, and the orbital pictures chemists use point along axes. Those pictures are the real orbitals, and they come from a simple freedom.

A degenerate level is a space: any combination is again a stationary state¶

If two functions solve the Schrödinger equation with the same energy, H^ψa=Eψa\hat{H}\psi_a = E\psi_aH^ψa​=Eψa​ and H^ψb=Eψb\hat{H}\psi_b = E\psi_bH^ψb​=Eψb​, then so does every combination:

H^ (caψa+cbψb)=caEψa+cbEψb=E (caψa+cbψb)\hat{H}\,(c_a\psi_a + c_b\psi_b) = c_aE\psi_a + c_bE\psi_b = E\,(c_a\psi_a + c_b\psi_b)H^(ca​ψa​+cb​ψb​)=ca​Eψa​+cb​Eψb​=E(ca​ψa​+cb​ψb​)
(7)

The 2l+12l + 12l+1 states of one nnn and lll share the energy EnE_nEn​ (and the eigenvalue ℏ2l(l+1)\hbar^2l(l+1)ℏ2l(l+1) of L^2\hat{L}^2L^2, which commutes with H^\hat{H}H^), so any combination of them is a stationary state with the same nnn and lll. The degenerate level is a (2l+1)(2l+1)(2l+1)-dimensional space, and Yl−l,…,YllY_l^{-l}, \dots, Y_l^{l}Yl−l​,…,Yll​ are one choice of axes in it. We may turn the axes, as Lecture 3.5 turned the axes of a matrix (Appendix A.3). The combinations are no longer eigenfunctions of L^z\hat{L}_zL^z​ (that operator does not care about nnn but does care about mmm), and that is the price of pointing them along xxx or yyy.

The real ppp orbitals¶

Pair mmm with −m-m−m. From the table of Lecture 4.4, Y1±1=∓3/8π sin⁡θ e±iϕY_1^{\pm1} = \mp\sqrt{3/8\pi}\,\sin\theta\,e^{\pm i\phi}Y1±1​=∓3/8π​sinθe±iϕ, and eiϕ+e−iϕ=2cos⁡ϕe^{i\phi} + e^{-i\phi} = 2\cos\phieiϕ+e−iϕ=2cosϕ, eiϕ−e−iϕ=2isin⁡ϕe^{i\phi} - e^{-i\phi} = 2i\sin\phieiϕ−e−iϕ=2isinϕ:

The real ppp orbitals
pz=Y10=34π cos⁡θ=34π zrp_z = Y_1^0 = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\,\cos\theta = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\,\frac{z}{r}pz​=Y10​=4π3​​cosθ=4π3​​rz​
(8)
px=Y1−1−Y1+12=34π sin⁡θcos⁡ϕ=34π xr,py=i (Y1−1+Y1+1)2=34π sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ=34π yrp_x = \frac{Y_1^{-1} - Y_1^{+1}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\,\sin\theta\cos\phi = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\,\frac{x}{r}, \qquad p_y = \frac{i\,(Y_1^{-1} + Y_1^{+1})}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\,\sin\theta\sin\phi = \sqrt{\frac{3}{4\pi}}\,\frac{y}{r}px​=2​Y1−1​−Y1+1​​=4π3​​sinθcosϕ=4π3​​rx​,py​=2​i(Y1−1​+Y1+1​)​=4π3​​sinθsinϕ=4π3​​ry​
(9)

  • Multiplied by Rn1(r)R_{n1}(r)Rn1​(r) they are the orbitals npxnp_xnpx​, npynp_ynpy​, npznp_znpz​: same nnn, same l=1l = 1l=1, same energy EnE_nEn​, same L2=2ℏ2L^2 = 2\hbar^2L2=2ℏ2

  • They are real, normalized and orthogonal, and each is the same shape pointed along a different axis: x/rx/rx/r, y/ry/ry/r, z/rz/rz/r

  • pxp_xpx​ and pyp_ypy​ have no definite LzL_zLz​: a measurement of LzL_zLz​ on pxp_xpx​ gives +ℏ+\hbar+ℏ or −ℏ-\hbar−ℏ, each half the time

Example: build pxp_xpx​

Add the two m=±1m = \pm1m=±1 harmonics with the signs of the table:

Y1−1−Y1+1=38πsin⁡θ e−iϕ+38πsin⁡θ e+iϕ=38πsin⁡θ (2cos⁡ϕ)=32πsin⁡θcos⁡ϕY_1^{-1} - Y_1^{+1} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{8\pi}}\sin\theta\,e^{-i\phi} + \sqrt{\frac{3}{8\pi}}\sin\theta\,e^{+i\phi} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{8\pi}}\sin\theta\,(2\cos\phi) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2\pi}}\sin\theta\cos\phiY1−1​−Y1+1​=8π3​​sinθe−iϕ+8π3​​sinθe+iϕ=8π3​​sinθ(2cosϕ)=2π3​​sinθcosϕ
(10)

Divide by 2\sqrt{2}2​: px=3/4π sin⁡θcos⁡ϕp_x = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\,\sin\theta\cos\phipx​=3/4π​sinθcosϕ, and rsin⁡θcos⁡ϕ=xr\sin\theta\cos\phi = xrsinθcosϕ=x. Normalization costs nothing: Y1−1Y_1^{-1}Y1−1​ and Y1+1Y_1^{+1}Y1+1​ are orthonormal, so ∣c−1∣2+∣c+1∣2=12+12=1\lvert c_{-1}\rvert^2 + \lvert c_{+1}\rvert^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} = 1∣c−1​∣2+∣c+1​∣2=21​+21​=1. The same two numbers are the probabilities of the two LzL_zLz​ readings. (Some books leave out the Condon-Shortley signs and write pxp_xpx​ as a sum; the densities agree.)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from matplotlib.colors import LightSource, to_rgb
th, ph = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, np.pi, 73), np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 145), indexing="ij")
st, ct, cp, sp = np.sin(th), np.cos(th), np.cos(ph), np.sin(ph)
x, y, z = st * cp, st * sp, ct
ls = LightSource(azdeg=300, altdeg=40)
pos, neg, dcol = np.array(to_rgb(TEAL)), np.array(to_rgb(ORANGE)), np.array(to_rgb(PURPLE))
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.6, 5.6))
def balloon(ax, dens, sign, lab):
    rho = dens / dens.max()
    fc = np.where(sign[..., None] >= 0, pos, neg) if sign is not None else np.broadcast_to(dcol, rho.shape + (3,))
    ax.plot_surface(rho * x, rho * y, rho * z, facecolors=fc, rstride=1, cstride=1, linewidth=0, antialiased=False, shade=True, lightsource=ls)
    for v, name, off in (((1.15, 0, 0), "$x$", (1.12, 0, 0)), ((0, 1.15, 0), "$y$", (0, 1.12, 0)), ((0, 0, 1.05), "$z$", (0.16, 0, 0.98))):
        ax.plot([0, v[0]], [0, v[1]], [0, v[2]], color="#868e96", lw=1.0)
        ax.text(v[0] * off[0] + off[0] * (v[0] == 0), v[1] * off[1] + off[1] * (v[1] == 0), v[2] * off[2] + off[2] * (v[2] == 0), name, fontsize=11, color="#495057", ha="center", va="center")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.9, 0.9); ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 0.9); ax.set_zlim(-0.9, 0.9)
    ax.set_box_aspect((1, 1, 1)); ax.view_init(elev=20, azim=-58); ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=14, y=0.97)
# top row: |Y_1^m|^2 for m = +1, 0, -1 (densities, purple: no sign to show)
for k, (m, lab) in enumerate(((1, r"$|Y_1^{+1}|^2$"), (0, r"$|Y_1^{0}|^2$"), (-1, r"$|Y_1^{-1}|^2$"))):
    ax = fig.add_subplot(2, 3, k + 1, projection="3d")

Fig. Top: the angular densities ∣Y1m∣2\lvert Y_1^m\rvert^2∣Y1m​∣2 of the three LzL_zLz​ eigenstates with l=1l = 1l=1, drawn as surfaces whose distance from the origin in each direction is the density in that direction: two rings and a dumbbell. Bottom: the three real orbitals pxp_xpx​, pyp_ypy​, pzp_zpz​, coloured by the sign of the wavefunction (teal positive, orange negative).

  • The two rings become two dumbbells. Nothing was added or lost: pxp_xpx​ and pyp_ypy​ span the same two-dimensional space as Y1+1Y_1^{+1}Y1+1​ and Y1−1Y_1^{-1}Y1−1​.

  • Each real ppp orbital has one nodal plane, where xxx, yyy or zzz is zero, and changes sign across it. The sign is not visible in the density, but it matters whenever two orbitals overlap: bonding in Chapter 8 is built on it.

  • These surfaces show the angular part only. They say nothing about size; the radial factor Rn1R_{n1}Rn1​ does that, and 2p and 3p have the same three shapes.

Running and standing waves¶

Why is the m=+1m = +1m=+1 density a ring but the pxp_xpx​ density two lobes? Watch the real part of each wavefunction in time, Re [ψ e−iEt/ℏ]\mathrm{Re}\,[\psi\,e^{-iEt/\hbar}]Re[ψe−iEt/ℏ], painted on a sphere as in Lecture 4.4:

Source
# synced: p_running
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from scipy.special import sph_harm_y
from matplotlib.colors import to_rgb
S = 221
u = np.linspace(-1, 1, S)
U, V = np.meshgrid(u, u[::-1])
inside = U**2 + V**2 < 1
W = np.sqrt(np.clip(1 - U**2 - V**2, 0, None))
el, az = np.radians(22), np.radians(-55)
cam = np.array([np.cos(el) * np.cos(az), np.cos(el) * np.sin(az), np.sin(el)])
ex = np.array([-np.sin(az), np.cos(az), 0.0])
ey = np.cross(cam, ex)
Pt = U[..., None] * ex + V[..., None] * ey + W[..., None] * cam
TH, PH = np.arccos(np.clip(Pt[..., 2], -1, 1)), np.arctan2(Pt[..., 1], Pt[..., 0])
light = np.array([-0.45, 0.55, 0.7]) / np.linalg.norm([-0.45, 0.55, 0.7])
shade = (0.5 + 0.5 * np.clip(U * light[0] + V * light[1] + W * light[2], 0, 1))[..., None]
white, pos, neg, dcol = np.ones(3), np.array(to_rgb(TEAL)), np.array(to_rgb(ORANGE)), np.array(to_rgb(PURPLE))
paint = lambda s: np.dstack([np.clip(np.where(s[..., None] > 0, white + s[..., None] * (pos - white), white - s[..., None] * (neg - white)), 0, 1) * shade, inside.astype(float)])
dens = lambda d: np.dstack([np.clip(white + d[..., None] * (dcol - white), 0, 1) * shade, inside.astype(float)])
Yp = sph_harm_y(1, 1, TH, PH)                                   # m = +1
px = ((sph_harm_y(1, -1, TH, PH) - Yp) / np.sqrt(2)).real       # p_x
top1, top2 = np.sqrt(3 / (8 * np.pi)), np.sqrt(3 / (4 * np.pi))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.0, 6.2), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.05, "hspace": 0.12})
ims = []
for row, (Y, top, lab) in enumerate(((Yp, top1, r"$Y_1^{+1}$"), (px, top2, r"$p_x$"))):
    ax, bx = axes[row]
    for a_ in (ax, bx):
        a_.set_xlim(-1.08, 1.08); a_.set_ylim(-1.08, 1.3); a_.set_aspect("equal"); a_.axis("off")
        a_.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), 1, fill=False, ec="#868e96", lw=0.8, zorder=3))
        a_.plot([0, 0], [ey[2], ey[2] + 0.28], color="#495057", lw=1.4, zorder=3)
        a_.text(0.07, ey[2] + 0.26, "$z$", fontsize=10.5, color="#495057", va="center")
    ims.append(ax.imshow(paint(Y.real / top), extent=(-1, 1, -1, 1), interpolation="bilinear", zorder=1))
    bx.imshow(dens(np.abs(Y)**2 / top**2), extent=(-1, 1, -1, 1), interpolation="bilinear", zorder=1)
    ax.text(-1.22, 0, lab, fontsize=15, ha="right", va="center")
axes[0, 0].set_title(r"Re $\psi(t)$", fontsize=13.5); axes[0, 1].set_title(r"$|\psi|^2$", fontsize=13.5)
frames = 30
def update(k):
    ph = np.exp(-1j * 2 * np.pi * k / frames)
    ims[0].set_data(paint((Yp * ph).real / top1))
    ims[1].set_data(paint((px * ph).real / top2))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.14, right=0.99, top=0.93, bottom=0.02)
ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=100, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())

  • Y1+1e−iEt/ℏ∝sin⁡θ ei(ϕ−Et/ℏ)Y_1^{+1}e^{-iEt/\hbar} \propto \sin\theta\,e^{i(\phi - Et/\hbar)}Y1+1​e−iEt/ℏ∝sinθei(ϕ−Et/ℏ) is a wave running around the zzz axis, the ring state of Lecture 4.4 wrapped on a sphere. Its real part turns; its density is the time average of a turning lobe pair, a ring.

  • px e−iEt/ℏ∝sin⁡θcos⁡ϕ e−iEt/ℏp_x\,e^{-iEt/\hbar} \propto \sin\theta\cos\phi\,e^{-iEt/\hbar}px​e−iEt/ℏ∝sinθcosϕe−iEt/ℏ is a standing wave: the lobes stay put along xxx and pulse between teal and orange. Its density is the two fixed lobes.

  • Both are stationary states of the same energy. The atom does not prefer one set; the question asked of it does. A magnetic field along zzz asks for LzL_zLz​ and picks the running waves; a neighbouring atom along xxx asks for direction and picks pxp_xpx​.

    ax.set_xlim(-0.9, 0.9); ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 0.9); ax.set_zlim(-0.9, 0.9)
    ax.set_box_aspect((1, 1, 1)); ax.view_init(elev=20, azim=-58); ax.set_axis_off()

Fig. The angular densities of the nine real orbitals with l≤2l \leq 2l≤2, coloured by the sign of the wavefunction. Every surface is drawn to the same largest radius; sizes are not compared here.

  • The names are the polynomials: rlYr^lYrlY for the real combinations is xxx, yyy, zzz for l=1l = 1l=1 and xyxyxy, yzyzyz, xzxzxz, x2−y2x^2 - y^2x2−y2, 3z2−r23z^2 - r^23z2−r2 for l=2l = 2l=2 (the row rlYlmr^lY_l^mrlYlm​ of the table in Lecture 4.4, recombined).

  • Four of the five ddd orbitals are the same four-leaf clover turned in space: dx2−y2d_{x^2-y^2}dx2−y2​ points its lobes along the xxx and yyy axes, dxyd_{xy}dxy​ between them, and dxzd_{xz}dxz​, dyzd_{yz}dyz​ stand the clover up in the xzxzxz and yzyzyz planes.

  • dz2d_{z^2}dz2​ is the odd one, two lobes along zzz and a ring, because m=0m = 0m=0 needs no partner. It is as much a ddd orbital as the others: Problem 3 shows that the clover and the ring share one L2L^2L2 and one energy, and a different choice of axis would turn one into the other.

  • Each real orbital with l=2l = 2l=2 has two nodal surfaces: two planes, or for dz2d_{z^2}dz2​ the two cones where 3z2=r23z^2 = r^23z2=r2. Each with l=1l = 1l=1 has one plane, and s has none.

Nodes: spheres, planes and cones¶

Put the two parts together. The complete orbital ψ=Rnl(r) Y(θ,ϕ)\psi = R_{nl}(r)\,Y(\theta, \phi)ψ=Rnl​(r)Y(θ,ϕ) vanishes wherever either factor does:

The nodes of an orbital
n−l−1⏟radial nodes: spheres Rnl(r)=0  +  l⏟angular nodes: planes or cones Y=0  =  n−1 nodal surfaces\underbrace{n - l - 1}_{\text{radial nodes: spheres } R_{nl}(r) = 0} \;+\; \underbrace{l}_{\text{angular nodes: planes or cones } Y = 0} \;=\; n - 1 \ \text{nodal surfaces}radial nodes: spheres Rnl​(r)=0n−l−1​​+angular nodes: planes or cones Y=0l​​=n−1 nodal surfaces
(11)

  • A radial node is a sphere on which ψ=0\psi = 0ψ=0: the electron is never found at that distance, in any direction

  • An angular node is a plane through the nucleus (or a cone around an axis) on which ψ=0\psi = 0ψ=0: never in that direction, at any distance

  • n−1n - 1n−1 in all, as the box state nnn has n−1n - 1n−1 nodes and the oscillator state vvv has vvv: more nodes, more bending, more kinetic energy, higher EnE_nEn​

The orbitals in three dimensions¶

Every real orbital with n≤3n \leq 3n≤3, as a cloud of positions drawn from ∣ψ∣2\lvert\psi\rvert^2∣ψ∣2 (each point coloured by the sign of ψ\psiψ), or as the boundary surface that encloses 90% of the probability. Cut an orbital open to see its spheres and planes from inside, and put every orbital in the same box to compare sizes.

What an orbital picture shows, and what it does not¶

pictureshowshides
radial distribution P(r)P(r)P(r)how far out the electron is, the radial nodes, the sizethe shape
angular surface ∣Y∣2\lvert Y\rvert^2∣Y∣2the shape and the angular nodesthe size, and the sign unless coloured
ψ\psiψ on a planesign, every node, sizethe other two dimensions
90% boundary surfacesize and shape togetherthe inside, the density, the tail beyond 90%
point cloudthe density itselfthe sign unless coloured, the nodes unless cut open

  • No picture is the orbital. The orbital is a function of three coordinates; each drawing projects one aspect of it. The textbook “shapes” are angular surfaces or boundary surfaces, and the “sizes” are 90% radii.

  • The sign is physics, not decoration. ∣ψ∣2\lvert\psi\rvert^2∣ψ∣2 hides it, but the overlap of two orbitals, ∫ψAψB dV\int\psi_A\psi_B\,dV∫ψA​ψB​dV, depends on it, and that overlap is bonding (Chapter 8). Drawings of ψ\psiψ colour the lobes; drawings of the density do not.

  • Real or complex is a choice of axes in a degenerate level. Nothing about the atom changes; what changes is which question the picture answers.

  • The next lecture adds what the Schrödinger equation left out: the electron’s own angular momentum, spin, which doubles every orbital and, in a magnetic field, separates the mmm states that this lecture combined (Spin).

Problems¶

Problem 1: Bohr’s radii return¶

For the states with l=n−1l = n - 1l=n−1 (1s, 2p, 3d, ...) the radial function is a single power times an exponential, R∝rn−1e−Zr/na0R \propto r^{n-1}e^{-Zr/na_0}R∝rn−1e−Zr/na0​. Show that the most probable distance of the electron is r=n2a0/Zr = n^2a_0/Zr=n2a0​/Z, the radius of Bohr’s nnnth orbit, and that the average distance is larger, ⟨r⟩=(n2+n/2) a0/Z\langle r\rangle = (n^2 + n/2)\,a_0/Z⟨r⟩=(n2+n/2)a0​/Z.

Solution

P(r)=r2R2∝r2ne−2Zr/na0P(r) = r^2R^2 \propto r^{2n}e^{-2Zr/na_0}P(r)=r2R2∝r2ne−2Zr/na0​. Set the derivative to zero:

dPdr∝(2n r2n−1−2Zna0 r2n)e−2Zr/na0=2n r2n−1(1−Zrn2a0)e−2Zr/na0=0⟹rmp=n2a0Z\frac{dP}{dr} \propto \left(2n\,r^{2n-1} - \frac{2Z}{na_0}\,r^{2n}\right)e^{-2Zr/na_0} = 2n\,r^{2n-1}\left(1 - \frac{Zr}{n^2a_0}\right)e^{-2Zr/na_0} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{\mathrm{mp}} = \frac{n^2a_0}{Z}drdP​∝(2nr2n−1−na0​2Z​r2n)e−2Zr/na0​=2nr2n−1(1−n2a0​Zr​)e−2Zr/na0​=0⟹rmp​=Zn2a0​​
(12)

For the average, normalize with ∫0∞rke−ar dr=k!/ak+1\int_0^\infty r^ke^{-ar}\,dr = k!/a^{k+1}∫0∞​rke−ardr=k!/ak+1 and a=2Z/na0a = 2Z/na_0a=2Z/na0​:

⟨r⟩=∫0∞r2n+1e−ar dr∫0∞r2ne−ar dr=(2n+1)!/a2n+2(2n)!/a2n+1=2n+1a=(2n+1) na02Z=(n2+n2)a0Z\langle r\rangle = \frac{\int_0^\infty r^{2n+1}e^{-ar}\,dr}{\int_0^\infty r^{2n}e^{-ar}\,dr} = \frac{(2n+1)!/a^{2n+2}}{(2n)!/a^{2n+1}} = \frac{2n + 1}{a} = \frac{(2n+1)\,na_0}{2Z} = \left(n^2 + \frac{n}{2}\right)\frac{a_0}{Z}⟨r⟩=∫0∞​r2ne−ardr∫0∞​r2n+1e−ardr​=(2n)!/a2n+1(2n+1)!/a2n+2​=a2n+1​=2Z(2n+1)na0​​=(n2+2n​)Za0​​
(13)

which is the general formula ⟨r⟩nl\langle r\rangle_{nl}⟨r⟩nl​ with l=n−1l = n - 1l=n−1. For 1s: rmp=a0r_{\mathrm{mp}} = a_0rmp​=a0​, ⟨r⟩=1.5 a0\langle r\rangle = 1.5\,a_0⟨r⟩=1.5a0​; for 3d: 9a09a_09a0​ and 10.5 a010.5\,a_010.5a0​. The most probable distance is Bohr’s radius exactly, for every nnn; the average is always a little larger because the distribution has a longer tail outward than inward.

Problem 3: Build dxyd_{xy}dxy​¶

Using Y2±2=15/32π sin⁡2θ e±2iϕY_2^{\pm2} = \sqrt{15/32\pi}\,\sin^2\theta\,e^{\pm2i\phi}Y2±2​=15/32π​sin2θe±2iϕ, show that (Y2+2−Y2−2)/(i2)(Y_2^{+2} - Y_2^{-2})/(i\sqrt{2})(Y2+2​−Y2−2​)/(i2​) is real, equals 15/4π xy/r2\sqrt{15/4\pi}\,xy/r^215/4π​xy/r2, and is normalized. What values of LzL_zLz​ can be measured in this state, with what probabilities? What is its L2L^2L2?

Solution
Y2+2−Y2−2=1532πsin⁡2θ (e2iϕ−e−2iϕ)=1532πsin⁡2θ (2isin⁡2ϕ)Y_2^{+2} - Y_2^{-2} = \sqrt{\frac{15}{32\pi}}\sin^2\theta\,\left(e^{2i\phi} - e^{-2i\phi}\right) = \sqrt{\frac{15}{32\pi}}\sin^2\theta\,(2i\sin2\phi)Y2+2​−Y2−2​=32π15​​sin2θ(e2iϕ−e−2iϕ)=32π15​​sin2θ(2isin2ϕ)
(14)

Divide by i2i\sqrt{2}i2​: the iii cancels and 2/2=22/\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{2}2/2​=2​, so the function is 15/16π sin⁡2θsin⁡2ϕ\sqrt{15/16\pi}\,\sin^2\theta\sin2\phi15/16π​sin2θsin2ϕ, real. With sin⁡2ϕ=2sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ\sin2\phi = 2\sin\phi\cos\phisin2ϕ=2sinϕcosϕ and rsin⁡θcos⁡ϕ=xr\sin\theta\cos\phi = xrsinθcosϕ=x, rsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ=yr\sin\theta\sin\phi = yrsinθsinϕ=y:

dxy=1516π⋅2 xyr2=154π xyr2d_{xy} = \sqrt{\frac{15}{16\pi}}\cdot2\,\frac{xy}{r^2} = \sqrt{\frac{15}{4\pi}}\,\frac{xy}{r^2}dxy​=16π15​​⋅2r2xy​=4π15​​r2xy​
(15)

Normalization: the two harmonics are orthonormal and the coefficients are ±1/(i2)\pm1/(i\sqrt{2})±1/(i2​), each of modulus squared 12\tfrac{1}{2}21​, summing to 1. Those same numbers are the probabilities: a measurement of LzL_zLz​ gives +2ℏ+2\hbar+2ℏ or −2ℏ-2\hbar−2ℏ, each with probability 12\tfrac{1}{2}21​, never 0 or ±ℏ\pm\hbar±ℏ. L2L^2L2 is sharp, ℏ2⋅2⋅3=6ℏ2\hbar^2\cdot2\cdot3 = 6\hbar^2ℏ2⋅2⋅3=6ℏ2, because both components have l=2l = 2l=2. The clover is a superposition of two rings running in opposite senses.

Problem 5: Is the electron ever at the nucleus?¶

P(r)P(r)P(r) vanishes at r=0r = 0r=0 for every state, yet ψ1s(0)≠0\psi_{1s}(0) \neq 0ψ1s​(0)=0. (a) Show that the density at the nucleus is ∣ψns(0)∣2=Z3/πa03n3\lvert\psi_{ns}(0)\rvert^2 = Z^3/\pi a_0^3n^3∣ψns​(0)∣2=Z3/πa03​n3 for s states and zero for every other lll. (b) Reconcile the two statements. (c) Why does the hyperfine splitting of hydrogen’s ground state (the 21 cm line of radio astronomy), which comes from the electron’s magnetic moment interacting with the proton’s at the proton’s position, exist for 1s but not for 2p?

Solution

(a) From the table of Lecture 5.1, Rn0(0)=2(Z/na0)3/2R_{n0}(0) = 2(Z/na_0)^{3/2}Rn0​(0)=2(Z/na0​)3/2 for every nnn (the polynomial equals 1 at ρ=0\rho = 0ρ=0 once the normalization is taken into account), and Y00=1/4πY_0^0 = 1/\sqrt{4\pi}Y00​=1/4π​, so

∣ψns(0)∣2=4Z3n3a03⋅14π=Z3πa03n3\lvert\psi_{ns}(0)\rvert^2 = \frac{4Z^3}{n^3a_0^3}\cdot\frac{1}{4\pi} = \frac{Z^3}{\pi a_0^3n^3}∣ψns​(0)∣2=n3a03​4Z3​⋅4π1​=πa03​n3Z3​
(16)

For l>0l > 0l>0, Rnl∝rlR_{nl} \propto r^lRnl​∝rl near the origin, so ψ(0)=0\psi(0) = 0ψ(0)=0: the centrifugal barrier of Lecture 5.1 keeps those electrons away. For hydrogen’s 1s the density at the proton is 1/πa03=2.1×10301/\pi a_0^3 = 2.1\times10^{30}1/πa03​=2.1×1030 m−3^{-3}−3, the largest anywhere in the atom.

(b) Both are true. The density is the probability per unit volume, largest at the nucleus; the radial distribution is the probability per unit length at distance rrr, which multiplies the density by the area 4πr24\pi r^24πr2 of a shell, zero at r=0r = 0r=0. The electron is found in a tiny ball around the nucleus with the small probability ∣ψ(0)∣2⋅43πϵ3\lvert\psi(0)\rvert^2\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi\epsilon^3∣ψ(0)∣2⋅34​πϵ3, not zero.

(c) The hyperfine interaction at the nucleus is proportional to ∣ψ(0)∣2\lvert\psi(0)\rvert^2∣ψ(0)∣2 (the Fermi contact term). It is nonzero only for s states, falls as 1/n31/n^31/n3, and vanishes for p, d, f. The 1s level of hydrogen splits by 5.9 μ5.9\,\mu5.9μeV, the 21 cm line; the 2p level has no contact splitting at all. For the same reason an s electron “sees” the nucleus in NMR couplings and in the isotope shifts of heavy atoms.

Problem 6: How big is 2p, and how big is He+^++?¶

(a) Show that the probability of finding a 2p electron inside a radius xxx (in a0a_0a0​) is 1−e−x(1+x+x22+x36+x424)1 - e^{-x}\left(1 + x + \tfrac{x^2}{2} + \tfrac{x^3}{6} + \tfrac{x^4}{24}\right)1−e−x(1+x+2x2​+6x3​+24x4​), by repeated integration by parts or by differentiating the result. (b) Solve numerically for the 90% radius and compare it with the 1s value 2.66 a02.66\,a_02.66a0​. (c) Without any new integral, give the 90% radii of 1s and 2p in He+^++ and Li2+^{2+}2+, and the most probable distances. (d) The ionization energy of He+^++ is four times hydrogen’s. Is its 1s electron four times, twice, or half as close to the nucleus on average?

Problem 7: Where does a pzp_zpz​ electron point?¶

An electron in a 2pz2p_z2pz​ orbital is measured for direction. (a) Find the probability that it is found within 30∘30^\circ30∘ of the zzz axis (above or below the nucleus). (b) Compare with an electron in 2s, which has no preferred direction. (c) What fraction of a 2pz2p_z2pz​ electron lies within 10∘10^\circ10∘ of the xyxyxy plane?

Solution

The angular distribution is ∣Y10∣2=34πcos⁡2θ\lvert Y_1^0\rvert^2 = \tfrac{3}{4\pi}\cos^2\theta∣Y10​∣2=4π3​cos2θ, and the direction does not depend on rrr, so the radial factor integrates to 1 and drops out.

(a) Both polar caps, 0≤θ≤θ00 \leq \theta \leq \theta_00≤θ≤θ0​ and π−θ0≤θ≤π\pi - \theta_0 \leq \theta \leq \piπ−θ0​≤θ≤π, with θ0=30∘\theta_0 = 30^\circθ0​=30∘:
